elements.quote: introduction: this paper updates and summarizes the current evidence informing rehabilitation of patients with coVid-19 and/or describing the consequences of the disease and its treatment.

elements.quote: introduction: this paper updates and summarizes the current evidence informing rehabilitation of patients with coVid-19 and/or describing the consequences of the disease and its treatment.

elements.quote: EVidEncE acQuisition: studies published from May 1 st to June 30 th , 2021 were selected, excluding descriptive studies and expert opinions.

The abstract does not identify the information sources used to find studies or when each source was last searched.

elements.quote: from this edition, we improved the quality assessment using the Joanna briggs institute checklists for observational studies and the cochrane risk of bias tool for randomized-controlled clinical trials (rcts).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the tools used to assess risk of bias/quality.

elements.quote: EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS: Twenty-five, out of 3699 papers, were included.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the evidence synthesis at least at a high level (narrative synthesis/results compilation).

elements.quote: EVIDENCE SYNTHESIS: Twenty-five, out of 3699 papers, were included. They were three RCTs, 13 cross-sectional studies and nine cohort studies. Twenty studies reported data on symptom prevalence (N.=13) or disease natural history (N.=7); and five studies reported intervention effectiveness at the individual level.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and summarizes study types, but it does not report total participants and only provides limited study-characteristic counts (e.g., N.=13 and N.=7).

elements.quote: Most studies in this updated review targeted the prevalence of limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest in coVID-19 survivors.... Twenty studies reported data on symptom prevalence (N.=13) or disease natural history (N.=7); and five studies reported intervention effectiveness at the individual level.
elements.reason: Main outcome domains are reported, but the abstract does not provide results for each main outcome with the number of included studies and participants per outcome (and participant counts are not shown).
The conditional element asks for meta-analysis summary estimates and intervals; the provided abstract evidence does not indicate that a meta-analysis was conducted.
The conditional element asks for direction of effect and which group is favored when groups are compared; the provided abstract evidence does not include such comparative results.

elements.quote: the most frequent risks of bias for rcts concerned weaknesses in allocation concealment, blinding of therapists, and lack of intention-to-treat analysis. Most analytical studies failed to identify or deal with confounders, describe or deal with dropouts or eventually perform an appropriate statistical analysis .
elements.reason: The abstract reports limitations related to risk of bias and methodological shortcomings of included evidence.

elements.quote: conclusions: Most studies in this updated review targeted the prevalence of limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest in coVID-19 survivors.... More rcts and analytical observational studies are available, but the methodological quality of recently published studies is low. There is a need for good quality intervention efficacy and effectiveness studies to complement the rapidly expanding evidence from observational studies.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation of findings and implications for future research.
The abstract evidence does not state the primary source of funding.
The abstract evidence does not provide the register name and registration number.

elements.quote: conclusions: Most studies in this updated review targeted the prevalence of limitations of functioning of rehabilitation interest in coVID-19 survivors. This is similar to past review findings; however, data in the new studies was collected at longer follow-up periods (up to one year after symptom onset) and in larger samples of participants. More rcts and analytical observational studies are available, but the methodological quality of recently published studies is low. There is a need for good quality intervention efficacy and effectiveness studies to complement the rapidly expanding evidence from observational studies.
elements.reason: The abstract describes what the existing evidence shows (focus on prevalence/natural history, low methodological quality) and identifies uncertainties/gaps (need for good quality intervention efficacy/effectiveness studies).

elements.quote: The best available research evidence is required to inform management and rehabilitation decisions, interventions, and health systems for COVID-19 survivors with adverse clinical sequelae. Further evidence is warranted to estimate the resources needed to plan for setting appropriate and adequately delivered post-acute and long-term rehabilitation services.
elements.reason: The introduction text explains why conducting/using the review evidence is important (to inform management/rehabilitation decisions and to estimate resources for post-acute/long-term services).

elements.quote: The literature search was comprehensive with the search strategy replicating previous review editions that, to date, have been the most complete investigations of rehabilitation evidence related to COVID in health literature.
elements.reason: The review states the search replicates previous review editions and that prior findings are similar, but the evidence provided does not clearly identify and cite specific “previous systematic reviews” (with explicit references) to justify the need for this current review/update.
No evidence was retrieved describing a proposed mechanism of action of the intervention(s) in the context of intervention effects.
No evidence was retrieved indicating that a logic model (for complex interventions/delivery contexts) is provided.
